name: Aligoté

lines.s10: Aligoté is Burgundy's other white grape: lean, lemony and bright, the wine that built the Kir and now stands alone.
lines.s20: Aligoté is Burgundy's second white grape, often planted at the top and the foot of Chardonnay's slopes. It gives a light, dry wine of lemon and green apple with a sharp, clean finish, the classic partner for blackcurrant liqueur in a Kir.
lines.s45: Many people have drunk Aligoté without knowing it, poured over blackcurrant liqueur as a Kir. It grows across Burgundy beside Chardonnay, often at the top and the foot of the slopes. On its own it tastes of lemon, green apple and a little acacia blossom. It is light, dry and brisk, with more bite than Chardonnay. Most of it sees steel, not new oak, and is sold young. Try it with oysters, snails in garlic butter or a slice of parsleyed ham. One village name, Bouzeron, is kept for it alone, and its golden strain has thin skins that turn gold as they ripen.
lines.sale: Aligoté is white Burgundy without the weight: lemon, green apple and a clean, sharp finish. I would pour it with anything in garlic butter, or with a little cassis as a Kir to open the evening.

glass.lead: Lemon, green apple and acacia blossom, lean and brisk, with a touch of hazelnut in riper wines.

ladder.where: Burgundy's hilltops and Hautes Côtes in most years
Bouzeron's marl slopes, and warm years across Burgundy

glass.structure: Dry. Acidity high, alcohol moderate, body light to medium; leaner and sharper than the Chardonnay grown beside it.

home.home: Burgundy, where it has grown since the seventeenth century and has held its own regional name, Bourgogne Aligoté, since 1937. It is often planted at the top and foot of the slopes and made in steel for drinking young. Bouzeron, on the Côte Chalonnaise, is the one village name reserved for it, and its golden strain gives a rounder wine.
home.abroad: It travelled east more than west: Bulgaria, Romania, Moldova, Ukraine and Russia all grow it. In the rest of the wine world it is a rarity.

service.temp: 45 to 50 degrees Fahrenheit, 7 to 10 degrees Celsius; Bouzeron a touch warmer.
service.glass: A white wine glass; a Kir is built in the same glass, cassis first.
service.decant: Usually unnecessary; serve it cold and fresh.
service.age: Enjoy it young, within two or three years; Bouzeron can keep a little longer.

with.dish: Snails in garlic and parsley butter
with.why: sharp acidity cuts the butter and garlic

labels.means: The regional Burgundy name for the grape, its own since 1937; white wine only.
A village of the Côte Chalonnaise whose wine is Aligoté alone, and tends to be rounder.
Golden Aligoté, the thin skinned strain of Bouzeron that turns gold as it ripens.
Crème de cassis topped with Bourgogne Aligoté; named for a mayor of Dijon.
Burgundy's sparkling wine, in which Aligoté may join Chardonnay and Pinot Noir.

guest.q: Is this the wine that goes into a Kir?
guest.a: Yes. A Kir is crème de cassis topped with Bourgogne Aligoté, whose sharpness balances the sweet liqueur. With Champagne it becomes a Kir Royale. The wine is well worth a glass on its own.

guest.q: How is it different from Chardonnay?
guest.a: It is lighter, leaner and sharper, with lemon and green apple, and it is seldom aged in new oak. Think of it as Burgundy's brisk white for the start of the meal.
A village in the Côte Chalonnaise, in the south of Burgundy, and the only village name kept for Aligoté. Its wines tend to be rounder, with a note of hazelnut.

compare.tell: Chardonnay is rounder and fuller, and often shows cream or toast from the cellar; Aligoté is leaner and sharper, with lemon and green apple.
Melon de Bourgogne, as Muscadet, is lighter still, with a salty, bready note from its lees; Aligoté has more lemon and more bite.
Pinot Blanc is softer and rounder, with ripe apple and almond at gentler acidity; Aligoté is sharper and more lemony.

profile.st: Pale straw gold with green tints · Body light to medium · Acid high · Alcohol moderate · Dry
profile.fruit: Lemon, lemon zest and green apple; ripe pear and white peach in Bouzeron and in warm years
profile.other: Acacia blossom, hawthorn and wet stone; a touch of hazelnut in riper wines; seldom any new oak
profile.tell: Lean, brisk white Burgundy of lemon and green apple with no cream or toast: lighter and sharper than Chardonnay
profile.regions: Burgundy: Bourgogne Aligoté across the region, Bouzeron in the Côte Chalonnaise; also Bulgaria, Romania, Moldova and Ukraine
profile.confuse: Chardonnay is rounder, with cream or toast from the cellar; Muscadet is lighter, saltier and bready; Pinot Blanc is softer, with almond

cards.front: Aligoté: where is it at home, and which village is kept for it?
cards.back: Burgundy, as Bourgogne Aligoté, a regional name of its own since 1937. Bouzeron, in the Côte Chalonnaise, is the one village name reserved for the grape.

cards.front: What goes into a Kir, and why does Aligoté suit it?
cards.back: Crème de cassis topped with Bourgogne Aligoté. The wine is dry, light and high in acidity, so it balances the sweet blackcurrant liqueur.

cards.front: Aligoté against Chardonnay in the glass: what parts them?
cards.back: Aligoté is lighter, leaner and higher in acidity, with lemon and green apple and seldom any new oak. Chardonnay is rounder and often shows cream or toast.

questions.q: A guest orders a Kir before dinner and asks which wine traditionally goes over the cassis. Which do you name?
questions.exp: A Kir is crème de cassis topped with Bourgogne Aligoté, whose high acidity balances the sweet liqueur. With Champagne it becomes a Kir Royale, and Petit Chablis and Mâcon-Villages are Chardonnay.

questions.q: A guest wants a white Burgundy that is not Chardonnay. Which village name on the list is made from Aligoté alone?
questions.exp: Bouzeron, in the Côte Chalonnaise, is the one village name reserved for Aligoté. The white wines of Rully, Montagny and Saint-Véran are all Chardonnay.

questions.q: Two white Burgundies are poured side by side. One is light and lean, all lemon and green apple, with sharp acidity and no trace of a barrel; the other is rounder, with cream and toasted hazelnut. Which grape made the first?
questions.exp: Lean, sharp and lemony with no barrel note is the mark of Aligoté. Chardonnay is the rounder glass beside it, and Burgundy's Sauvignon Blanc, from Saint-Bris, would smell of cut grass and gooseberry.

A record I believe is wrong: the region question r-rkgv0zwg says Bouzeron became a village appellation in 1997. The decree is dated 17 February 1998 by Bourgogne Wines and the national institute, though one page of the trade body also says 1997. The entry gives no year, so nothing shown disagrees.
Service temperature follows the Codex's row for light whites, 45 to 50 degrees Fahrenheit; Bourgogne Wines itself suggests 11 to 12 degrees Celsius.
The Kir is named for a mayor of Dijon, as the Codex's own service reference words it, with no person named.
Left out: its parents, Pinot and Gouais Blanc, as a spoken hook, since Melon de Bourgogne closes on the same fact; the Melon card names Aligoté among the siblings.
Left out: how the wines of Bulgaria, Romania, Moldova, Ukraine and Russia taste; the sources confirm only that the grape is grown there.
The sources were read through search results; this session could not open the hosts directly.

checked.verdict: Sound after four fixes. The seventeenth century, 1937, Bouzeron and its thin skinned golden strain were confirmed.
changed: lines.s20, lines.s45, worlds.home and the ladder: often on the higher slopes becomes the top and the foot of the slopes. Two references say the grape is relegated to the highest and the lowest ground while Chardonnay and Pinot Noir keep the middle; only in Bouzeron is it said to hold the upper slopes.
lines.s45: under a splash of blackcurrant liqueur becomes poured over blackcurrant liqueur, as the Codex's own service reference builds a Kir, cassis first.
lines.s45: One village, Bouzeron, is given over to it becomes One village name, Bouzeron, is kept for it alone. The village also grows Chardonnay and Pinot Noir under other names.
glass.ladder, the moderate rung: Bouzeron's sheltered slopes becomes Bouzeron's marl slopes. Shelter stood on no source; white marl does.
open: The author's flag stands: the Codex gives 1997 for Bouzeron, in question r-rkgv0zwg and in the Burgundy reading, while the decree is dated 17 February 1998. The entry gives no year.
